objectives.title: Where are the blue crabs?
objectives.scenario: Resource managers want to compare blue crab distribution and relative abundance across the Hudson River estuary.
objectives.objective: Compare blue crab occurrence and relative abundance among regions and habitats.
objectives.clue: Think about spatial coverage, habitat accessibility, season, gear selectivity, and replication.
objectives.discussion: If catches differ among regions, how will you know it is not simply because you sampled them differently?

objectives.title: Where are the nursery habitats?
objectives.scenario: Managers want to identify Hudson River habitats used by juvenile striped bass during early life stages.
objectives.objective: Compare juvenile striped bass occurrence and relative abundance among habitat types.
objectives.clue: Life stage matters. Your gear and timing must actually sample juvenile fish.
objectives.discussion: Does catching more juveniles in one habitat prove that it is a better nursery compared to another?

objectives.title: Can you find a rare species?
objectives.scenario: Scientists need information about Atlantic sturgeon occurrence and habitat use while minimizing disturbance.
objectives.objective: Detect Atlantic sturgeon and describe where and when detections occur.
objectives.clue: Use noninvasive approaches. Rare species may require repeated effort and broad coverage.
objectives.discussion: If you detect zero sturgeon at a station, does that prove they never use it?

objectives.title: What happens when the river changes?
objectives.scenario: Managers suspect fish distribution is related to temperature, salinity, and dissolved oxygen.
objectives.objective: Design a survey that links fish occurrence or abundance with environmental conditions.
objectives.clue: Biological and environmental observations should be collected at comparable places and times.
objectives.discussion: How could season or habitat create an apparent relationship between fish and temperature?

objectives.title: Did restoration work?
objectives.scenario: A Hudson River shoreline has been restored. Managers want to know whether juvenile fish use increased after restoration.
objectives.objective: Evaluate whether juvenile fish occurrence changed following restoration.
objectives.clue: Include at least one unrestored reference site and think about before/after comparisons.
objectives.discussion: If fish increase at the restored site, what evidence would suggest restoration, not a river-wide change, was responsible?

gear.limitation: Catch depends on fish behavior and angler skill

Move through these five decisions in order. You can go back and revise as your budget changes.

Where will you sample—and how many stations?
Which gear can actually answer your question?
When, how often, and how many repeats?
What will you measure, and can you afford it?
Tip: A strong survey is not the one that spends the most money. It is the one whose choices match the research objective.
Your background information and species profiles are available to help you make informed survey design decisions.
